objectives: Conclude the Article XXVIII negotiation with the UK by June, on terms Brussels can approve, so the Council can vote on the final implementing act on schedule
Prevent the UK from joining Japan and Korea in a joint FTA dispute or any coordinated disapplication of FTA provisions in retaliation — this is a core risk to manage throughout

Preserve the EU's ability to set the TRQ architecture (volume, allocation method, administration) that works for the final domestic legislation, while offering the UK enough predictability of access to make settlement worthwhile
Avoid giving the UK terms so generous that they become a benchmark that inflates the parallel claims from Turkey, Korea, India and Japan

Protect the EU's long-term standing in Geneva: conduct the process procedurally cleanly, maintain a working relationship with my UK counterpart across the wider Goods file, and avoid reputational damage from the FTA disapplication text

Keep linkage options open — particularly the interaction between UK access under the EU TRQ and EU exporters' treatment under the UK's own steel measure — without letting the negotiation collapse into an unmanageable swap
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a settlement is reached within four rounds that (a) gives the UK materially better and more predictable access than the fallback (larger quota and/or country-specific allocation and/or carve-outs for UK-concentrated product lines), (b) preserves the 50% out-of-quota rate and the permanent legal footing the EU needs, (c) takes the joint FTA dispute off the table, ideally by softening or dropping the FTA-disapplication text for the UK, and (d) does not create precedents that blow up the Turkey/Korea/India/Japan tracks. Partial success: no settlement, but the process was visibly reasonable, the UK refrains from joining the FTA dispute, and retaliation stays within Article XXVIII bounds. Failure: no settlement plus UK joins a coordinated FTA dispute with Japan and Korea, or UK retaliation escalates beyond substantially equivalent concessions — that would damage both the file and my standing as the EU's Geneva goods representative.
declaration.approach: Open by signalling procedural seriousness and continuity of the bilateral relationship, then get the UK's full position on the table before offering anything — I have no settlement figure from Brussels, so Round 1 is for listening and reporting. My likely negotiating shape: hold the 50% out-of-quota rate as a red line (it is the notified modification and Brussels says it proceeds), but trade on quota volume, allocation method and administration — a country-specific share or licence-based allocation gives the UK the predictability that first-come-first-served denies, at modest real cost to the EU. Use the FTA-disapplication text as the key concession: it is legally and reputationally the weakest part of the EU package, and offering to soften or drop it for the UK is the cheapest way to buy off the joint dispute risk and generate goodwill, since it costs the EU little in tariff revenue relative to the UK relationship. Explore quiet reciprocity on the UK's own steel measure (EU exporters currently hold country-specific quotas there) as a natural parallel, but keep it informal to avoid TCA contamination. Throughout, keep the tone cooperative with my UK counterpart — we work together on the whole Goods file — while making clear to Brussels that the FTA text is the single biggest escalation risk and should be traded early rather than defended to the end.

parties.who: UK Geneva counterpart (UK Mission, Department for Business and Trade)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum tariff-free tonnage with predictable allocation (country-specific quota sized near historic 2.4Mt flows), carve-outs for the narrow product range where UK exports concentrate, removal of the FTA-disapplication text, a review clause, and quiet assurance that joining Japan/Korea in a dispute stays credible as leverage

A defensible political outcome for a concentrated domestic steel industry: either a large quota or a strong retaliation narrative; will weigh whether settlement beats the fallback of withdrawing equivalent concessions against EU imports

parties.who: Brussels (Commission DG TRADE / Council via Trade Policy Committee)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Conclusion by June, no undermining of the 50% rate or the permanent legal footing, containment of the parallel Turkey/Korea/India/Japan claims, and no precedent that weakens the EU's position on non-market overcapacity
A tight quota, global FCFS allocation, no carve-outs, and minimal compensation — they want the UK inside a small quota competing with everyone else

parties.who: EU steel-consuming member states and manufacturers
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Adequate import volumes at low duty; more relaxed about a larger TRQ or licensing, though quiet about it

parties.who: Japan and Korea (with Turkey and India)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: To watch the UK-EU track for precedents; Japan and Korea are actively trying to recruit the UK into a joint FTA dispute — I expect them to counsel the UK against early settlement and to demand at least as good terms in their own tracks
Procedural propriety under Article XXVIII; many will quietly sympathise with the UK on the FTA-disapplication text, which affects the EU's broader reputation on the Goods file I manage long-term

objectives: Conclude an Article XXVIII settlement with the UK in time for the June Council vote, so the steel regime is not left legally and politically exposed.
Preserve the core protective effect of the notified regime: very high out-of-quota protection at or near 50%, tight control of in-quota volumes, strong administration and anti-circumvention rules.
Keep total preferential or zero-duty access for the UK far below its historic 2.4 million tonnes, ideally through a capped share inside the global TRQ rather than an additive UK-specific quota.
Defend the principle that FTA tariff reductions do not undermine the modified bound rate, while allowing at most a small, shared, tightly conditioned FTA pool if needed to close.
Avoid concessions that create easy precedents for Turkey, Korea, India and Japan, or that provoke member states, downstream users or the European Parliament to block implementation.
Use linkage to the UK's own steel measure to secure orderly treatment for EU exporters and reduce the risk of UK retaliation after any settlement or non-settlement.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success means both capitals accept the same terms by round four and the Council can vote in June: the 41 lines remain covered, out-of-quota protection remains prohibitive, zero-duty access is capped well below historic UK flows, administration is licensable and enforceable, any FTA pool is small and shared, review language cannot reopen the regime easily, compensation outside steel is minimal, and the UK commits not to retaliate and to treat EU exporters predictably under its own measure. Failure means no settlement and a delayed implementing act, or a settlement that effectively restores UK access, gives the UK a large guaranteed country quota, abandons the FTA disapplication principle, creates copycat demands from other suppliers, triggers broad compensation, or leaves the regime politically unstable in Council.
declaration.approach: Open firm and technical, not theatrical. I will make clear that the modification will proceed and that the June Council timetable is real, while framing no-deal as damaging to both sides and especially awkward for the UK despite the UK's six-month retaliation lever. I will anchor on overcapacity, permanence and enforceability, then trade only inside a narrow envelope: keep the 50% out-of-quota rate; any increase above 400,000 tonnes must be inside a single controlled volume, not stacked with extra UK or FTA pools; prefer licensing with quarterly limits, product sub-limits, no generous carry-over, melt-and-pour or equivalent origin discipline and suspension for circumvention; any UK reassurance is expressed as access under the global TRQ or a capped FTA/TCA pool shared with others, not as a bilateral guarantee; review only if evidence-based and not automatic. I will concede first on administration and predictability, then cautiously on volume, never on product coverage or legal principle unless the UK gives equivalent value through non-retaliation, cooperation under the TCA and commercially meaningful treatment for EU exporters in the UK measure. I will keep the Trade Policy Committee tightly briefed so the package remains sellable to steel member states without alarming steel-consuming member states, and I will use US retaliation noise as a reason for disciplined closure rather than as a reason to soften the regime.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum tariff-free access for UK steel, ideally a country-specific quota near historic flows, restoration of FTA preference, product carve-outs for concentrated UK export lines, low out-of-quota rate, early review and leverage from linkage to EU access under the UK steel measure.

parties.who: UK capital, Department for Business and Trade and ministers
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A politically defensible deal that protects steel jobs and avoids a no-deal shock, but with enough flexibility to blame EU intransigence if talks fail; they will fear missing a deal more than they admit because the EU market absorbs most UK exports.

A June-concludable package that visibly cuts imports, protects steel-producing member states, does not impose heavy costs on steel-consuming manufacturers, avoids compensation on sensitive lines and does not expose the EU to escalation with the UK or US.
Delivery of the mandate, no missed Council deadline, containment of US retaliation risk, legal durability at the WTO and no loss of control over the design of the EU steel import regime.
A small quota, high out-of-quota rate, strict origin and circumvention rules, no FTA backdoor, long duration and rapid enforcement against diverted volumes.
Adequate import supply, predictable licensing, product-specific flexibility, lower risk of retaliation and no abrupt cost shock from an overly restrictive quota.
Separate but watchful claims; they will exploit any UK-specific generosity, FTA pool design or compensation precedent to demand equal or better treatment in their own Article XXVIII processes.
An excuse to pressure or retaliate against the EU; not a formal party to the UK negotiation but relevant to timing, burden-sharing and the EU's tolerance for a prolonged no-deal.
Preservation of their preferential position and clear differentiation from the UK and other FTA partners, especially if any FTA pool is created.

objectives: Secure a country-specific quota allocation for the UK sufficient to protect the majority of the 2.4 million tonnes of UK steel exports to the EU, ideally through a dedicated UK share reflecting historical trade flows rather than a global first-come first-served quota that would be exhausted by larger suppliers
Resist or substantially narrow the EU's proposed disapplication of FTA tariff reductions for UK-origin steel, as this cuts access below even MFN treatment and would be devastating to the UK industry
Reduce the out-of-quota bound rate from 50% and/or increase the TRQ volume from 400,000 tonnes
Obtain a review clause and defined duration rather than a permanent open-ended measure

Preserve a working relationship with the EU counterpart across the wider goods file and avoid escalating into a tit-for-tat that could damage the UK's own Article XXVIII process and safeguard measure, under which EU exporters hold country-specific quotas
Keep London accurately informed so that any settlement put to Ministers is credible, deliverable and defensible
declaration.success_and_failure: Success means a settlement that gives the UK a meaningful, predictable share of tariff-free access — ideally a country-specific allocation covering a substantial portion of historical exports, a lower out-of-quota rate, the FTA disapplication removed or softened, and a review clause — while leaving the EU-UK working relationship intact for the many other goods files I handle. Failure means either no settlement by the end of round four (leaving the UK facing the original 50%/400,000t global FCFS proposal and the destruction of much of UK steel exports), or a settlement so weak that London would regard it as capitulation. A middling outcome that preserves workable access and the bilateral relationship is acceptable; a no-deal that I could have prevented through realistic negotiation is not.
declaration.approach: I will open by making clear that the EU's first proposal is not a serious basis for negotiation and would devastate UK steel, while signalling that the UK wants an early settlement and recognises the EU's June Council timeline — that timeline is my main leverage. I will probe what the EU is actually prepared to move on: volume, allocation method, country-specific shares, the FTA disapplication, and compensation on other lines. I will trade where there is genuine reciprocity — notably treatment of EU exporters under the UK's own steel safeguard measure, where the EU holds country-specific quotas — without ever linking files in a way that poisons the broader relationship. I will hold the Japan/Korea joint FTA dispute option in reserve as pressure but avoid committing to it early, since it would disrupt the negotiation and my credibility in Geneva committees. I will be candid with London about the realistic landing zone so that capital's instructions converge with what is actually achievable in the room.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A concluded Article XXVIII negotiation before the June Council vote; enough steel protection to satisfy producing member states; to keep the TRQ small and the out-of-quota rate high; to retain the FTA disapplication aimed at non-market economy circumvention; minimal compensation; and to avoid the UK withdrawing equivalent concessions that would hit EU steel exporters who currently enjoy country-specific quotas under the UK's own measure.

parties.who: UK capital (Department for Business and Trade / Ministers)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Protection of the UK steel industry and the 75% of exports that go to the EU; a country-specific allocation and removal of the FTA disapplication; credible retaliation options if talks fail; no settlement figure given, so they will rely on my reporting to judge what is acceptable; domestic political pressure from steel-producing constituencies.

Steel-producing member states want maximum protection and a hard line on overcapacity; steel-consuming manufacturing member states want cheap imports and a larger TRQ; collectively they need a package the Council can approve in June, which constrains how far the Commission can move late in the negotiation.

parties.who: Turkey, Korea, India, Japan (parallel Article XXVIII claimants)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Their own compensation from the EU; Japan and Korea want the UK to join a joint FTA dispute to pressure the EU, which would strengthen their hand but risks disrupting my negotiation; Turkey and Korea ship larger volumes than the UK and would dominate a global FCFS quota, which is my strongest argument for a country-specific UK share.

parties.who: UK steel industry and steel-region constituencies
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Survival: predictable duty-free access to the EU market covering most of current export volumes; they will judge any settlement harshly if it leaves them exposed to a global quota consumed by larger exporters.

objectives: Maximise continued tariff-free access for UK steel to the EU, prioritising a UK-specific zero-duty quota as close as possible to the 2.4 million tonne recent average rather than a share of a 400,000 tonne global quota.
Replace first-come first-served with stable administration, preferably licensing based on historic trade, so UK producers can plan and invest.
Remove or neutralise the proposed legal text disapplying FTA/TCA tariff reductions for UK-origin steel; preserve EU-UK TCA discipline and non-discrimination.
Reduce the out-of-quota bound rate below 50%, add a short duration and review clause, and seek carve-outs for the most vulnerable UK product lines.
Use improved EU country-specific allocations under the UK's own steel safeguard only as conditional leverage for significant EU concessions, not as a goodwill gesture.
Keep retaliation and the domestic subsidy option credible and ready, while using them to improve terms rather than as a first move.
Conclude by June only if the package is investable for UK steel; otherwise preserve a strong Article XXVIII non-agreement position and retaliation file.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a legally clean package that keeps the two at-risk plants investable: ideally a UK-specific zero-duty allocation around 1.8-2.2 million tonnes with historic-licence administration, out-of-quota rate no higher than about 25%, duration/review discipline, no FTA/TCA disapplication, targeted carve-outs, and any UK safeguard improvements strictly reciprocal and time-limited. A mixed success is a slightly lower quota if paired with a lower out-of-quota rate, review, TCA protection and a credible domestic subsidy bridge. Failure is acceptance of anything close to 400,000 tonnes global first-come first-served at 50%, FTA reductions disapplied, no review, or UK safeguard concessions granted without steel access gains; also failure if no deal leaves us without a prepared substantially-equivalent withdrawal list and a coherent plant-survival plan.
declaration.approach: Open by rejecting the notified architecture as non-compensatory and discriminatory, anchor high on a UK-specific quota based on historic trade, and make administration and TCA legal text core issues rather than technical afterthoughts. Sequence concessions: movement on UK safeguard allocations only after the EU moves on quota volume, allocation method, out-of-quota rate and FTA text. Exploit the EU's June deadline, open domestic implementing act and split member-state interests by offering a workable, precedent-limited bilateral solution that does not bind the separate Turkey/Korea/India/Japan claims. Keep instructions to Geneva tight: no settlement authority below thresholds without ministerial clearance; every offer must be conditional, reversible and drafted into the Article XXVIII record. Prepare in parallel a retaliation list against EU exports and the subsidy package so a no-deal outcome is credible, while signalling preference for a negotiated permanent footing.

parties.who: European Commission Article XXVIII negotiator in Geneva
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A mandate-compatible settlement by June that looks permanent and defensible, minimises compensation, avoids EU retaliation, preserves flexibility toward other claimants, and dresses the 50%/400,000 tonne model as reasonable while testing whether the UK will trade away leverage cheaply.

parties.who: Council / Trade Policy Committee and member states
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Producer states will want maximum protection and few exceptions; steel-consuming manufacturing states will fear input costs and may tolerate a larger TRQ, licensing and review; collectively they want no late crisis before the Council vote and no precedent that complicates other Article XXVIII claims.

Clear red lines, credible fallback authority, disciplined drafting instructions, and advance warning of any linkage between the EU TRQ and UK safeguard quotas so nothing is conceded at the table without capital approval.

parties.who: UK ministers and Secretary of State
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A politically defensible result that can be presented as saving steel jobs and sovereignty over trade defence, with no appearance of capitulation to Brussels and no unexplained concessions to EU exporters.

parties.who: UK steel producers and owners of the two at-risk plants
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Bankable certainty: meaningful zero-duty volume, stable allocation, protection from circumvention, a rate low enough to keep EU customers, and a timeline that justifies investment rather than closure.

Adequate import supply and predictable costs; they will resist a deal that protects producers so tightly that downstream manufacturing loses competitiveness, so safeguards and subsidies must be balanced.

Separate but watchful claims; larger suppliers will resist any UK-specific carve-out that shrinks their residual access, and all will exploit any EU precedent on global FCFS, country shares or compensation.

parties.who: EU steel exporters to the UK
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Preservation or expansion of their country-specific UK safeguard quotas; they are the UK's most concrete source of leverage and will lobby Brussels if their UK access is at risk.

public_message: The modification will proceed, but we want to conclude an Article XXVIII package that is defensible and avoids wider damage. As an opening, we can move from the notified global first-come-first-served approach toward country-specific administration by licence inside an enlarged pool: total pool of 1.8 million tonnes, with a UK-specific tranche of 1.0 million tonnes, out-of-quota bound rate held at 50% for now, five-year duration, and a review in year three. We are prepared to discuss product carve-outs, quarterly licence windows, a newcomer reserve, melt-and-pour enforcement, and compensation elsewhere in the EU schedule once we have agreed the steel architecture. Nothing is agreed until everything is agreed. I would also propose we keep the FTA-disapplication drafting under discussion rather than allowing it to spill into a broader TCA dispute.

other_terms: Licence-based administration using representative historical trade, with quarterly release windows and a 10% newcomer reserve
UK tranche inside the total pool, not additional to it; utilization and reallocation rules to be agreed
Possible carve-outs for narrow high-value or low-volume product lines after exchange of HS8 data
Melt-and-pour certification, anti-circumvention cooperation and no transhipment through third countries to access the UK tranche
Compensation on other EU schedule lines to be scoped after the steel TRQ architecture is fixed
FTA/TCA interaction language to be discussed separately with a view to avoiding cross-retaliation or a joint FTA dispute
Sequencing: data and methodology first, quota/administration second, compensation and legal drafting third

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A firm rejection of 1.0 million tonnes as far below the 2.4 million tonne average, a demand for a larger UK-specific share, opposition to any FTA-disapplication text, and pressure for a lower out-of-quota rate.
expectations.why: The UK has principal supplying interest and concentrated exposure; it must show industry it extracted more than the notified 400,000 tonnes global FCFS.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A harder public line than Geneva, but private interest in licensing, predictability and avoiding simultaneous escalation while the UK runs its own steel Article XXVIII affecting EU exporters.
expectations.why: Ministers need a defendable result quickly, yet EU-origin imports are also important to UK users and the UK has its own measure to protect.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Continued encouragement to the UK to make the FTA-disapplication element a joint FTA dispute rather than treating it as part of Article XXVIII compensation.
expectations.why: They want to widen the issue beyond steel compensation and increase leverage on the EU while their own claims remain separate.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Pressure to keep the opening disciplined, avoid naming a settlement figure, and report whether the UK prioritises volume, allocation method, FTA language or compensation on other lines.
expectations.why: The Council timeline is tight and several member states have conflicting steel-producing and steel-consuming interests.

private_rationale: Open materially above the notified 400,000 tonnes to look credible and prevent immediate escalation, but stay far below UK average trade because Brussels has given no settlement figure and the Council has not fixed the domestic act. Country-specific licensing is the main concession: it gives the UK predictability, is administrable, and can be presented as compensation without yet moving the 50% bound rate. Keeping the out-of-quota rate at 50% preserves leverage and avoids pre-empting member-state politics. Putting FTA/TCA language explicitly under discussion aims to separate it from the Korea/Japan joint-dispute track while not conceding it. The proposal is structured so the next round reveals UK priorities before the EU spends real concessions.

public_message: Thank you — movement toward country-specific administration is noted and welcome as direction of travel. But I have to be direct: the figures on the table are not a basis we can build on. The UK ships 2.4 million tonnes a year to the EU, three-quarters of our total steel exports. A 1.0 million tonne tranche inside a 1.8 million tonne pool would cut our tariff-free access by more than half, and on the current drafting the FTA disapplication provision removes the residual TCA preference on top. That is not compensation for withdrawing a zero bound rate on 41 lines; it is a managed contraction of the UK industry. We are a principal supplying interest, and the benchmark under Article XXVIII is substantially equivalent value. On our numbers, equivalence starts at preserving existing volumes: a UK tranche of 2.4 million tonnes, in a pool sized to reflect actual trade for all principal suppliers — we suggest 4.5 million tonnes — allocated country-specifically by licence with quarterly windows and a rollover mechanism for unused quarterly allocations. The out-of-quota bound rate needs to come down materially; 50% is a prohibitive rate, not a bound tariff. We propose 10%. Duration of three years with a review at 18 months and a presumption of adjustment to trade flows, not five years locked in. On the FTA disapplication text: we cannot treat that as a side conversation. Disapplying TCA tariff reductions to UK-originating steel while offering a quota is taking with one hand and compensating with the other. That provision needs to be withdrawn from the package, or this negotiation will not conclude. We are open on product carve-outs for hot-rolled coil feeding downstream processing, on melt-and-pour enforcement, and on discussing compensation lines once the steel architecture is credible. And I would note for the record that the UK and the EU face the same overcapacity problem from the same sources — this negotiation should not become a transfer of that pressure onto UK mills. Finally, we will need any package to take proper account of the treatment of EU exporters under the UK's own measure, and we are prepared to discuss that here in good faith.

other_terms: Withdrawal of the FTA-disapplication provision for UK-originating steel; TCA preferences to apply within and alongside the quota
Quarterly licence windows with rollover of unused allocations between quarters
Product carve-outs for hot-rolled coil and other inputs to UK-EU downstream processing supply chains
Melt-and-pour enforcement provisions
Review at 18 months with adjustment to tranche sizes based on actual trade flows
Compensation on other EU schedule lines to be scoped once steel architecture agreed
Parallel discussion of EU exporter treatment under the UK steel measure

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A counter that moves the UK tranche up from 1.0m but nowhere near 2.4m — likely 1.2-1.4m — possibly paired with a modest pool increase and an offer of carve-outs or compensation lines to make the tonnage gap palatable. Out-of-quota rate likely to hold near 50% with only token movement.
expectations.why: The EU has signalled flexibility on architecture but is constrained by its Council mandate and by parallel claims from Turkey and Korea, whose volumes exceed the UK's; conceding 2.4m to the UK would blow up its pool arithmetic and set a precedent for the other PSI negotiations.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Confirmation that 2.4m is the anchor, guidance on the minimum acceptable tranche, and a steer on how hard to press the FTA-disapplication withdrawal versus trading it for tonnage. Possibly a warning about Japan/Korea pressure for a joint dispute.
expectations.why: London asked me to establish what the EU is prepared to offer; my counter sets the ceiling of the conversation and London will need to define the floor before later rounds.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Renewed lobbying for a joint FTA dispute now that the EU has kept the disapplication text alive 'under discussion'.
expectations.why: The EU's proposal to keep the drafting on the table rather than withdraw it vindicates their concern and gives them an argument that quiet negotiation is not working.

private_rationale: The EU's opening moves on structure (country-specific, licensing, review) but the numbers are roughly 40% of our trade volume and the FTA disapplication would compound the loss. My instructions say the opening offer is far from the landing zone and to establish what the EU will actually offer, so I counter high but on defensible ground: the equivalence benchmark tied to actual trade volumes (2.4m), not an arbitrary number. Anchoring the pool at 4.5m is consistent with Turkey and Korea shipping more than us, so it is internally credible rather than rhetorical. The 10% out-of-quota rate and 3-year duration leave obvious concessions in my pocket for later rounds — I can trade duration and rate movement before I trade tonnage. Making FTA-disapplication withdrawal a headline demand serves two purposes: it is genuinely necessary (otherwise the quota value is undercut), and it gives Japan/Korea a reason to see bilateral negotiation working, buying time against the joint-dispute pressure without me committing to it. Flagging the UK measure and EU exporters' country-specific quotas signals I have a lever the EU wants, without explicitly linking them yet — that linkage is my strongest card and I should not play it in round one. Risk: London may think I have overreached on the pool; but post seats never settle, and a high, principled anchor preserves space for the capital seats to land later.

report: Round 1 opened with our proposed architecture: 1.8Mt pool, 1.0Mt UK tranche, country-specific licensing, 50% out-of-quota, five years, review in year three, with FTA disapplication drafting kept under discussion. The UK welcomed the move to country-specific allocation but rejected the figures outright. Their counter: UK tranche of 2.4Mt (i.e. full preservation of historic volumes), pool of 4.5Mt, out-of-quota rate of 10%, three-year duration with review at 18 months and a presumption of adjustment to trade flows. Two structural points matter more than the numbers. First, the UK has made withdrawal of the FTA-disapplication provision a condition of conclusion — their words were that the negotiation 'will not conclude' otherwise. This is consistent with the whisperings about Japan and Korea seeking a joint FTA dispute; the UK is signalling it has that lever and is prepared to be associated with it. Second, the UK explicitly linked this negotiation to the treatment of EU exporters under the UK's own steel measure — a threat and an opportunity in the same sentence. Constructive elements: they accept licensing with quarterly windows, proposed a rollover mechanism for unused allocations, and are open on carve-outs for hot-rolled coil feeding downstream processing, melt-and-pour enforcement, and compensation lines once the architecture is credible. The negotiating space is real but wide. Nothing was agreed.

recommendation.reasoning: There is no basis to accept anything close to the UK's ask — 2.4Mt tranche, 10% out-of-quota and an open-ended adjustment presumption would gut the measure and set an impossible precedent for the Turkey, Korea, India and Japan claims. But walking away is worse: failure means the 400kt global first-come-first-served fallback applies to our closest steel partner, near-certain UK retaliation against 3.6Mt of EU exports, and materially raises the risk of the joint UK-Japan-Korea FTA dispute. The UK's engagement on administration (licensing, quarterly windows, rollover, melt-and-pour) shows they want a deal. My recommended next move is to concede on the FTA-disapplication provision for the UK — it is legally exposed, it is the lightning rod for the joint dispute, and it costs us little in protective terms — in exchange for the UK moving well below 2.4Mt, accepting an out-of-quota rate no lower than 20-25%, and dropping the automatic adjustment presumption in favour of a review with defined criteria. We should also probe whether improved security for EU exporters under the UK measure can be priced into a larger UK tranche. We have four rounds and a June Council deadline; we should aim to have the architecture agreed by end of Round 3.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Mandate flexibility to move the UK tranche up to approximately 1.6-1.8Mt within a pool of up to 3.0Mt, strictly conditional on UK movement on the out-of-quota rate, duration and the review mechanism.
requests.why: Our 1.0Mt opening has been rejected as a non-starter and I have no settlement figure. Without headroom I cannot make a credible second move and we will burn a round.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: A Council-level decision on the FTA-disapplication provision: authority either to withdraw it for UK-originating steel, or to withdraw it entirely, as part of the final package.
requests.why: The UK has made this a condition of conclusion, and it is the provision most likely to trigger the joint UK-Japan-Korea FTA dispute. Dropping it entirely may actually de-escalate the Korea and Japan files as well. I need to know what I can put on the table in Round 2.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Guidance on whether we may link this negotiation to the UK's own steel measure, and if so what we want: at minimum, preservation of current EU country-specific quota allocations and a consultation commitment before any tightening.
requests.why: The UK raised this linkage themselves. It is our best source of leverage to buy a larger UK tranche at lower cost to the measure, but I cannot trade on it without instructions.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: A view on precedent management: how far a country-specific UK tranche can go before it undermines our position with Turkey and Korea, who ship larger volumes.
requests.why: Every tonne we give the UK country-specifically will be cited in the parallel Article XXVIII claims. I need to know the ceiling Brussels can defend across all five files, not just this one.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Confirmation that the June Council timeline still holds and that a settlement in Round 3 or 4 can be ratified on schedule.
requests.why: If the timeline slips, our incentive to settle early weakens and so does the UK's; I need to calibrate how much urgency to show at the table.

private_rationale: Frankly, the 1.0Mt opening was never going to survive contact with a principal supplying interest shipping 2.4Mt — the UK's reaction was predictable and their red line on FTA disapplication is credible, not theatrical. My real assessment of the landing zone: UK tranche somewhere between 1.6 and 1.9Mt, pool around 3Mt, out-of-quota 20-25%, four years, review with defined criteria but no automatic adjustment. The FTA disapplication provision is the cheapest major concession we hold — it is legally fragile under the TCA, it is what converts a routine Article XXVIII into a multi-member FTA dispute, and surrendering it may buy us both a lower UK tranche and insulation from the Japan-Korea manoeuvre. The danger points: (1) the UK's 10% out-of-quota ask — if capital is tempted toward it, the measure ceases to function; (2) the 'presumption of adjustment' — this is an open-ended ratchet and must be resisted in any settlement; (3) if we go country-specific and generous for the UK, Turkey and Korea will demand equivalent treatment and the pool arithmetic gets very tight. I have not said any of this at the table. I also note the UK counterpart was disciplined and constructive on process — this is negotiable if Brussels gives me room. My standing with the UK seat across the Goods file is an asset here; I would rather spend some of it than hand them a grievance that outlives this negotiation.

requests.why: Our 1.0Mt opening has been rejected as a non-starter and I have no settlement figure. Without headroom I cannot make a credible second move and we will burn a round.

requests.why: The UK has made this a condition of conclusion, and it is the provision most likely to trigger the joint UK-Japan-Korea FTA dispute. Dropping it entirely may actually de-escalate the Korea and Japan files as well. I need to know what I can put on the table in Round 2.

requests.why: The UK raised this linkage themselves. It is our best source of leverage to buy a larger UK tranche at lower cost to the measure, but I cannot trade on it without instructions.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: A view on precedent management: how far a country-specific UK tranche can go before it undermines our position with Turkey and Korea, who ship larger volumes.

instruction: Good opening. Your read is correct: the UK wants a deal, and the linkage they offered on their own measure is the most valuable currency in this room. For Round 2, do not move the headline figures yet. Hold 1.8Mt pool / 1.0Mt UK tranche as our position, but signal that we see scope to revisit volumes once the UK moves off 2.4Mt and off 10% out-of-quota. Your stated conditions for any volume movement: out-of-quota rate no lower than 20-25%, duration of at least four years, and a review clause with defined criteria (import penetration, capacity utilisation, global overcapacity indicators) — explicitly no presumption of automatic adjustment. On the FTA disapplication text: you are authorised to say that the EU is prepared to address it as part of a final package, but not to withdraw it unilaterally or this round — it is the UK's stated red line, so it must buy us the maximum. Table the linkage on their own measure: we want preservation of existing EU country-specific quota allocations under the UK safeguard and a commitment to consult before any tightening. Present this as part of the overall balance, and probe whether a larger UK tranche is available in exchange. Accept their technical agenda — quarterly windows, rollover, melt-and-pour, carve-outs for HRC feeding downstream processing — these cost us little and build momentum. Do not accept the 4.5Mt pool framing; anchor on a pool sized by reference to the measure's protective purpose, not historic trade.

authority.notes: These are ceilings/floors, not Round 2 positions. Do not table 1.6Mt / 2.8Mt / 25% in Round 2 — hold for Round 3 and trade volume only against UK movement on out-of-quota rate, duration, and the review mechanism. Out-of-quota rate must not go below 20% under any circumstances. No automatic adjustment presumption in the review clause — defined criteria only. FTA disapplication withdrawal may be offered only as part of a complete final package, not as a standalone concession; prefer withdrawal limited to UK-originating steel, with full withdrawal for all FTA partners as fallback if it closes the deal. Any agreement on volumes is conditional on UK commitments regarding treatment of EU exporters under the UK measure: preservation of current EU country-specific quota allocations plus a consultation commitment before any tightening. Quarterly licensing, rollover of unused allocations, newcomer reserve, melt-and-pour enforcement and HRC carve-outs for downstream processing are all acceptable and may be conceded freely as goodwill.

private_rationale: The 1.0Mt opening was deliberately low and has done its job — it anchored the UK at 2.4Mt, which is a maximalist ask we can trade down from. The real settlement zone is probably 1.4-1.6Mt UK tranche, 2.4-2.8Mt pool, 25% out-of-quota, 4-5 years, review with criteria, FTA disapplication withdrawn for the UK, and reciprocal security for EU exporters under the UK safeguard. The FTA disapplication provision was always expendable — it was included partly as a bargaining chip and its withdrawal now costs us nothing while buying the UK's red line. The US retaliation threat is the main reason not to gamble on no-deal despite our analysts' assessment that the UK suffers more; a June failure compounds with the US file in a way member states will not accept. Biggest risk: the UK pockets our Round 2 signals without moving off 2.4Mt — hence the instruction to hold figures and trade only conditional movement.

report: Round 1 complete. The EU moved early and substantively off its notified position: global first-come-first-served replaced by country-specific licence administration, inside an enlarged pool of 1.8m tonnes with a UK-specific tranche of 1.0m tonnes. Out-of-quota rate held at 50%, five-year duration, review in year three. They flagged openness on product carve-outs, quarterly licence windows, a newcomer reserve, melt-and-pour enforcement, and compensation lines elsewhere in the schedule — but only once the steel architecture is agreed. They explicitly proposed keeping the FTA-disapplication drafting inside this negotiation and away from a broader TCA dispute. I responded that the numbers are not a basis to build on: 1.0m tonnes is less than half our current 2.4m tonnes of trade, and with the FTA disapplication text still live it amounts to a managed contraction of UK steel, not compensation under Article XXVIII. I tabled our opening architecture: UK tranche of 2.4m tonnes in a 4.5m tonne pool, country-specific licence allocation with quarterly windows and rollover of unused quarterly allocations, out-of-quota bound rate of 10%, three-year duration with review at 18 months and a presumption of adjustment to trade flows. I stated plainly that the FTA disapplication provision must be withdrawn from the package or the negotiation will not conclude — this was delivered as a stated condition, visible to the EU. I also put on the table our openness on carve-outs for hot-rolled coil feeding downstream processing, melt-and-pour enforcement, and linkage to treatment of EU exporters under our own measure. Overall assessment: the EU's move on allocation method and pool size in round one signals real negotiating room and their June timeline pressure is genuine. But the gap on volumes (1.0m vs 2.4m) and out-of-quota rate (50% vs 10%) remains very wide, and the FTA disapplication text is the most dangerous element — if it survives, even a large quota is worth less than it appears. The EU signalled they want to sequence steel architecture first and compensation later; we should resist closing architecture without compensation at least scoped.

recommendation.reasoning: We cannot accept anything near 1.0m tonnes — that destroys the industry and London has been clear on that. But walking away in round one forfeits the EU's early movement and leaves us with the worst-case default: 400,000 tonnes global first-come-first-served, which is catastrophic for us. The EU has already conceded the allocation principle and moved the pool up more than fourfold from the notified 400,000. The right play is to hold our volume anchor, concede nothing on the FTA disapplication red line, and begin identifying which elements we can trade: duration (we could live with five years if volumes and the FTA text are right), the newcomer reserve, quarterly windows, and possibly a UK tranche below 2.4m if paired with a low out-of-quota rate, guaranteed TCA preference, and meaningful compensation lines. We should also quietly value the linkage they have invited on treatment of EU exporters under our own measure — that is a real concession we hold, given EU-origin steel is 64% of our finished imports. I recommend continuing, holding the stated position, and seeking in round 2 a material move on the UK tranche and withdrawal of the FTA disapplication text as the price of us engaging on compensation and duration.

instruction: Round 2 strategy: hold the public architecture you tabled — 2.4m UK tranche, 10% out-of-quota rate, FTA disapplication withdrawn — but do not repeat it so rigidly that the EU prices us as intransigent. Your objective this round is to extract the EU's second move on tonnage and to force the FTA disapplication text onto the table as a negotiating item, not a backdrop. Signal clearly, in descending order of cheapness, what we can move on: (1) administration — we will engage seriously on quarterly licence windows, a modest newcomer reserve, and melt-and-pour enforcement now; (2) duration — we can live with five years if the review clause has teeth, meaning an explicit adjustment mechanism tied to actual trade flows and utilisation, not a talking shop; (3) review timing — 18 months vs year three is tradeable. Do NOT move on the UK tranche figure this round. Do NOT move on the 10% out-of-quota rate beyond acknowledging the gap exists. On the FTA disapplication text: restate that it must be withdrawn for the package to conclude, but you may now invite the EU to explain what they would need in return for withdrawing it — that converts our red line into their problem to price. On compensation: agree to begin scoping compensation lines in parallel with the steel architecture, not after it; accept their sequencing only if they move materially on volume this round. On the UK safeguard linkage: you may confirm, in principle and without figures, that improved treatment of EU exporters under the UK measure is available as part of a balanced package — do not put numbers on it yet, and make clear it is contingent on conclusion here and cannot be banked separately. On the EU's June timeline: use it. They need conclusion more than they are showing. If the EU comes back with anything below 1.5m tonnes for the UK tranche, treat it as non-responsive and say so.

authority.notes: UK tranche floor of 1.8m tonnes is your private settlement floor — do not reveal it. Target landing zone is 2.0-2.2m tonnes with out-of-quota rate of 15-20%. You may accept five-year duration only if the review clause includes a binding adjustment mechanism responsive to trade flows and quota utilisation. Withdrawal of the FTA disapplication text is a red line for rounds 2-3; any softening of that position requires fresh Ministerial clearance — its only conceivable trade is dormant-status drafting (text suspended for the full duration, never activated) in exchange for a UK tranche at or above 2.2m tonnes AND an out-of-quota rate at or below 15% AND meaningful compensation lines, and even that must come back to London first. Compensation on other EU schedule lines must be scoped in parallel from round 2 onward. Any offer on EU exporters' allocations under the UK safeguard measure must remain conditional, reciprocal, and coordinated with our own Article XXVIII team — you may discuss shape, not tonnage.

response_to_requests.request: A settlement envelope: minimum UK tranche, maximum out-of-quota rate, and whether FTA disapplication withdrawal is an absolute red line.
response_to_requests.why: Minimum acceptable UK tranche: 1.8m tonnes, and only with a review mechanism with teeth plus compensation elsewhere. Anything below 1.5m is politically undeliverable and would not keep the two at-risk plants viable; below that, Ministers would prefer no agreement, withdrawal of substantially equivalent concessions, and the subsidy route. Maximum acceptable out-of-quota rate: 25%, and only if paired with a tranche at or near 1.8m; target 15-20%. On your worked example: 1.6-1.8m with 15-25% and FTA text withdrawn is acceptable only at the top of that range (1.8m/15-20%) plus compensation; 1.6m fails without exceptional compensation. On the FTA disapplication text: treat it as an absolute red line in rounds 2-3. Privately, it is our single most valuable card after the safeguard linkage — it is tradeable only for dormant-status drafting plus a package at or above 2.2m tonnes and 15% or below, and only with Ministerial clearance. Do not let the EU learn it is tradeable before round 4, if ever.

response_to_requests.why: You are authorised to offer improved country-specific quota allocations for EU exporters under the UK safeguard in exchange for significant EU concessions — specifically a UK tranche materially above 1.8m and/or a materially lower out-of-quota rate. Limits: the offer must be conditional on conclusion of this Article XXVIII package, framed as a rebalancing of existing EU allocations and modest enlargement rather than new access, and coordinated live with the team running our own Article XXVIII process so the two negotiations do not undercut each other. Confirm availability in principle in round 2; no figures before round 3, and then only against concrete EU movement on tonnage. This card spends once.

response_to_requests.request: Guidance on handling Japan and Korea's pressure to join a joint FTA dispute on the disapplication provision.
response_to_requests.why: Your instinct is correct. Hold them at arm's length: express sympathy for their concerns, note that the provision is a live item in our negotiation, make no commitment to joint action, and do not join any joint dispute while this negotiation is live. Joining would harden the EU's position on the very text we are trying to get withdrawn and would collapse the EU's offer to keep the matter out of a broader TCA dispute. If asked directly, our line is that the UK reserves all rights and is pursuing the matter in the Article XXVIII channel in the first instance. Capital-level conversations are not happening on this; nothing will contradict you.

response_to_requests.request: A view on how far you may go on duration, review mechanics and administration as soft concessions.
response_to_requests.why: These are our cheapest currency and you should spend them visibly and early to buy tonnage. Duration: full flexibility between three and five years — concede five years gladly if the review clause carries a binding adjustment mechanism tied to trade flows and utilisation. Administration: quarterly licence windows, rollover of unused quarterly allocations, and melt-and-pour enforcement are all acceptable now. Newcomer reserve: acceptable if small (low single-digit percentage of the pool) and not carved out of the UK tranche. Use each concession incrementally and announce each as movement requiring reciprocity — the EU's next move must be on the UK tranche.

private_rationale: The EU's round-one move confirms they have real room and real time pressure; their opening of 1.0m/50% is a classic anchor and we should expect a landing zone somewhere in the 1.5-2.0m range if we hold. Our floor of 1.8m is calibrated to plant viability: below that the Minister's judgment is that the subsidy programme becomes cheaper politically than defending the deal, and the no-agreement default (400k global FCFS plus our right to withdraw concessions) gives us genuine, if painful, leverage — the EU exports 3.6m tonnes to us and holds country-specific allocations under our measure, which they will not want jeopardised. The two cards we must not spend early are the FTA disapplication text (their ask, our red line — let them pay to remove their own provision) and the safeguard linkage (our only direct leverage over their exporters). The main risk this round is the EU pocketing our administrative and duration flexibility without moving on tonnage; the instruction is designed to make every soft concession visibly conditional. The secondary risk is Ministers discovering the floor exists; it stays in this channel. If round 2 produces no movement on the tranche, we should consider letting the EU's June deadline work harder by slowing rounds 3-4.

reasoning: Round 1 produced opening positions only, with no agreed terms on the table to accept. The UK's counter (2.4Mt tranche, 4.5Mt pool, 10% out-of-quota, three years with automatic adjustment presumption) is unacceptable — it would hollow out the measure's protective purpose and set an impossible precedent for the parallel Turkey, Korea, India and Japan claims. But the UK has signalled genuine negotiating space: they accept country-specific licensing, quarterly windows, rollover, melt-and-pour enforcement and carve-outs, and they have themselves offered linkage to the treatment of EU exporters under the UK measure — our most valuable source of leverage. Their red line on the FTA disapplication provision is a known quantity that we hold in reserve to trade only as part of a complete final package. With four rounds available and authority in hand up to 2.8Mt pool / 1.6Mt UK tranche / 25% out-of-quota / four years, the correct course is to continue: hold the headline figures in Round 2, concede the low-cost technical agenda, table the UK-measure linkage, and bank volume movement for Round 3 in exchange for UK movement on the out-of-quota rate, duration and a criteria-based review. Accepting now would settle on nothing; defaulting now would sacrifice the June Council timeline and invite UK retaliation plus a possible joint FTA dispute.

The terms on the table — a 1.0m tonne UK tranche inside a 1.8m tonne pool, 50% out-of-quota rate, and the FTA disapplication text still live — would cut UK tariff-free access by more than half and are politically and industrially undeliverable, falling well short of the Article XXVIII benchmark of substantially equivalent value against a zero bound rate on 41 lines. However, the EU's round-one movement off its notified position (country-specific allocation, a pool enlarged more than fourfold, openness on administration and carve-outs) shows genuine negotiating room under real time pressure, and walking away now would leave the catastrophic default of 400,000 tonnes global first-come-first-served. The correct course is to hold our stated architecture, press for a material second EU move on tonnage and withdrawal of the FTA disapplication text, and begin trading our cheapest concessions — administration, duration, review mechanics — while keeping the safeguard linkage and compensation lines in reserve.

public_message: Thank you. Let me respond on substance, because I think we can make progress on the architecture even where the headline numbers remain far apart. On administration, we can close a good deal today: the EU accepts quarterly licensing windows, a rollover mechanism for unused quarterly allocations, a newcomer reserve, melt-and-pour enforcement, and product carve-outs for hot-rolled coil feeding downstream processing. Consider those agreed in principle as the technical chassis of the package. On the FTA-disapplication drafting: I have heard you clearly that this is a condition of conclusion, not a side conversation. I am not in a position to withdraw it unilaterally today, but I can say formally that the EU is prepared to address it as part of a complete final package. It is in the negotiation, and it will be resolved here — provided the overall balance warrants it. On volumes and rates, I have to be equally direct: a UK tranche of 2.4 million tonnes with a 10% out-of-quota rate is not a modification of our schedule, it is the absence of one. The measure exists because of global overcapacity, and an out-of-quota bound rate of 10% would leave the EU market open to precisely the diverted flows this instrument is designed to manage — and it would be cited line by line in the parallel claims from other suppliers. Equally, a review clause must operate against defined criteria — import penetration, capacity utilisation, global overcapacity indicators — not a presumption of automatic adjustment to trade flows. What I can say is that we see scope to revisit both the pool and the UK tranche once you move off 2.4 million tonnes and off 10%. That scope is real, but it is conditional: out-of-quota rate in a defensible range, duration of at least four years, and a criteria-based review. Finally, you raised the treatment of EU exporters under your own measure, and we welcome that. We are prepared to discuss it here as part of the overall balance: our interest is preservation of existing EU country-specific quota allocations under the UK safeguard and a commitment to consult before any tightening. If there is genuine security for EU exporters on your side of the ledger, that changes what is possible on ours. My formal position for this round therefore stands as tabled — 1.8 million tonne pool, 1.0 million tonne UK tranche, country-specific licensing, 50% out-of-quota, five years, review in year three — but everything I have just said about conditionality is on the record, and I would invite you to test it in the next round.

expectations.why: UK steel production is concentrated in a few sites with significant employment; ministers cannot concede the rate before they can present volume gains, which is why we held figures this round while showing the pathway.

private_rationale: Brussels instructed me to hold headline figures this round and trade volume only against UK movement on rate, duration and the review mechanism — so the formal position stays at 1.8Mt/1.0Mt/50%/5yr even though I have authority up to 2.8Mt/1.6Mt/25%/4yr. The alternatives were (a) table a real volume move now — rejected because it spends my best currency before the UK has moved off 2.4Mt or 10%, and because the FTA-disapplication provision must buy maximum value as their stated red line; or (b) hold rigidly with no signal — rejected because the UK explicitly said the current figures are 'not a basis to build on' and a second round with no visible pathway risks hardening their linkage to the Japan/Korea joint dispute track. Instead I banked the entire technical agenda as agreed-in-principle (it costs us nothing and creates momentum and sunk-cost commitment), put the FTA-disapplication provision formally inside the negotiation but only as part of a complete final package, tabled the linkage to the UK measure as our price for a larger tranche, and made the volume conditionality explicit and on the record — out-of-quota in a defensible range, four-plus years, criteria-based review. This gives the UK capital something to sell internally (a real pathway to bigger volumes) while preserving every element of my Round 3 envelope. Key risks to manage: the UK may read the held figures as intransigence and escalate the joint-dispute rhetoric; and the 50% out-of-quota rate is now clearly our biggest gap — at some point I will need to move toward 25% to keep them at the table, which Brussels has authorised as a floor of 20% but prefers 25%.

public_message: Thank you — that was a substantive response, and I want to bank progress where it exists. On the technical chassis, we agree: quarterly licensing windows, rollover of unused quarterly allocations, a newcomer reserve, melt-and-pour enforcement, and product carve-outs for hot-rolled coil feeding downstream processing are agreed in principle. That is real, and I will report it to London as such. On duration, I am authorised to move: the UK can accept five years, provided the review clause is not a talking shop. We need a binding adjustment mechanism — defined triggers tied to quota utilisation and actual trade flows, with an obligation to adjust volumes when triggers are met, not merely to discuss them. If your criteria — import penetration, capacity utilisation, overcapacity indicators — can sit alongside those triggers in the review text, we can close duration and review together. On the FTA-disapplication drafting: I note it is formally in the negotiation, and I note you cannot withdraw it today. So let me convert this constructively: what would the EU need, within this package, for that text to be withdrawn? I am inviting you to price it, because it cannot survive into a concluded agreement. On volumes and rates: I acknowledge the gap, as you have acknowledged yours. But I would ask you to apply the same test you applied to me — a 50% out-of-quota bound rate on lines currently bound at zero is not a modification either, it is a wall, and a UK tranche of 1.0 million tonnes against 2.4 million tonnes of actual trade is not substantially equivalent value under Article XXVIII by any arithmetic I can defend in London. Our architecture stands at 2.4 million tonnes and 10% — and yours stands at 1.0 and 50. Neither of us concludes there. The scope you described as real and conditional: I am testing it now. For round three I need a material move on the UK tranche and on the rate — and I will be candid that movement measured in tens of thousands of tonnes will not register as a response. On compensation: we agree to begin scoping other lines in parallel from now, and I would propose our teams exchange indicative lists before the next round. Finally, on your exporters under our measure: I can confirm in principle that security for EU country-specific allocations, and consultation before any tightening, is available within a balanced concluded package — shape, not tonnage, at this stage, and it cannot be banked separately from conclusion here. If the next round brings a credible volume and rate move, I am prepared to put more specificity on that than I have today.

report: Round 2 closed with genuine movement on structure but no convergence yet on numbers. On the FTA-disapplication text: the UK converted their red line into a constructive demand — they formally invited me to price its withdrawal within the package. This is an opportunity: it means withdrawal is tradeable currency rather than a precondition in limbo, and it defers (for now) the Japan/Korea joint-dispute risk. On volumes and rates: neither side moved. I held 1.8Mt/1.0Mt/50%/5yr as instructed; they hold 2.4Mt/10%. The UK explicitly warned that movement 'measured in tens of thousands of tonnes will not register' in Round 3 — they need a material move to justify their own climbdown, and their language suggests they have room to move if we do. On compensation: agreed to exchange indicative lists of other lines before Round 3 — teams to start now. On their own measure: they confirmed in principle that security for EU country-specific allocations plus consultation before tightening is available within a balanced concluded package — but it cannot be banked separately from conclusion. That linkage is now formally live and priced as 'shape, not tonnage.' Overall: the deal shape is visible — five years, criteria-plus-triggers review, country-specific licensing, FTA text withdrawn as part of the final package, mutual security on both measures — with the fight concentrated on tranche size and out-of-quota rate.

This move should be explicitly conditioned on: UK dropping from 2.4Mt toward the 1.6-1.8Mt zone, UK moving from 10% toward 20%+, and acceptance of the review architecture. Duration of five years can now be closed — the UK has conceded it and it exceeds our four-year floor — in exchange for agreement on the trigger mechanism. I would also recommend formally pricing the FTA-disapplication withdrawal this round: withdrawal limited to UK-originating steel, contingent on (a) UK acceptance of an out-of-quota rate of at least 20%, (b) UK tranche within our final range, and (c) written commitments on preservation of EU allocations and pre-tightening consultation under the UK measure. Offering it now as a priced, conditional element — rather than in the final package — tests UK seriousness and lets us bank their counter-movement before we actually concede the text.

instruction: Round 2 was well played. The technical chassis is banked, the UK has moved three-to-five years on duration, and their red line on the FTA text is now tradeable currency rather than an ultimatum. Proceed as follows in Round 3. (1) Volumes and rate: table 2.2Mt pool / 1.3Mt UK tranche / 35% out-of-quota. Present it explicitly as a material response to their test — a 30% increase in the tranche — and condition it in the same breath on UK movement off 2.4Mt and off 10%. Do not move beyond these figures this round under any circumstances; 1.6Mt / 2.8Mt / 25% remains the Round 4 endgame and 20% is the absolute rate floor. (2) Duration and review: you may now close five years. On the trigger mechanism, you may accept an obligation to adjust volumes when defined triggers are met, provided: triggers are objective, quantified in the text, and symmetric (adjustment up or down); any adjustment operates within pre-agreed bands, not open-ended recalibration to trade flows; and our import-penetration, capacity-utilisation and overcapacity criteria sit alongside utilisation and trade-flow triggers. That is a criteria-based binding review, not an automatic adjustment presumption — frame it that way to the TPC. Do not accept triggers tied solely to historic trade volumes or any mechanism with a ratchet in only one direction. (3) FTA-disapplication text: you are authorised to price it. Offer withdrawal limited to UK-originating steel, expressly contingent on a concluded package containing: out-of-quota rate at or above 20%, UK tranche within the range you table, and written UK commitments on preservation of existing EU country-specific quota allocations under their measure plus consultation before any tightening. Make clear this pricing lapses if the package does not conclude. Full withdrawal for all FTA partners remains reserved as the closing fallback and is not to be disclosed as available. (4) Their measure: press for specificity this round — they said 'shape, not tonnage'; ask them to put the shape on paper. (5) Compensation: teams may exchange indicative lists. Signal scope on selected industrial lines where our defensive exposure is low; no commitments, no line-by-line discussion at the table, and nothing banked until the steel architecture is agreed. Nothing is agreed until everything is agreed remains our formulation.

Duration of five years is now acceptable and may be closed. Review clause may include a binding obligation to adjust when objective, quantified, symmetric triggers are met, with adjustments confined to pre-agreed bands and combined with import-penetration/capacity-utilisation/overcapacity criteria; no automatic presumption, no one-directional ratchet, no trigger set based solely on historic trade volumes. FTA-disapplication withdrawal may be priced now as a conditional offer limited to UK-originating steel, contingent on rate ≥20%, tranche within range, and written UK commitments on EU allocations plus pre-tightening consultation under the UK measure; full withdrawal for all FTA partners is reserved as undisclosed closing fallback. response_to_requests.request: Mandate decision on accepting binding, trigger-based obligation to adjust volumes in the review clause
response_to_requests.why: The UK conceded three-to-five years; refusing any binding adjustment would forfeit that and expose the review as cosmetic, which the TPC cannot defend either. Granted with strict limits: triggers must be objective, quantified, and symmetric; adjustments confined to pre-agreed bands; our protective criteria must sit alongside utilisation and trade-flow triggers. This is distinguishable from an automatic adjustment presumption and I will defend it to the TPC on that basis. If the UK demands open-ended recalibration or one-way ratchets, the answer is no and duration reverts to four years.

response_to_requests.why: Granted. They asked us to price it; pricing it now converts their red line into a transaction on our terms and buys movement on rate and volume before we concede anything. UK-originating steel only at this stage, strictly contingent on the rate floor, the tranche range, and written commitments on their measure. Full withdrawal stays undisclosed — it may be worth more on the Korea and Japan files than here, and I will not spend it twice.

If they pocket the 1.3Mt and do not move off 2.4Mt or 10% in the same round, hold everything and let Round 4 be the reckoning — the June deadline pressures them at least as much as us.

response_to_requests.why: Granted in limited form. No commitments, no quantification, and nothing banked until the steel architecture is agreed. Compensation is a balancing tool, not a substitute for discipline on tranche and rate.

response_to_requests.request: Update on the parallel Turkey, Korea, India and Japan files, including precedent pricing and Korea/Japan reaction to possible withdrawal of the disapplication text
response_to_requests.why: For your calibration only, not for the table: a UK country-specific tranche in the 1.3-1.6Mt range is absorbable across the five files provided we frame it against the UK's concentrated product mix and the TCA relationship rather than raw volume — Turkey and Korea ship more but across broader ranges, and their claims will be sized accordingly. Do not let the UK learn this ceiling is considered absorbable. On the disapplication text: withdrawing it entirely would materially de-escalate the Korea and Japan files, which is precisely why full withdrawal is reserved and UK-only withdrawal is the priced offer. The internal discussion on a shared preferential pool for FTA partners continues; no volume has been agreed, and a UK tranche at the top of our range will draw objections from others — another reason to hold 1.3Mt this round.

private_rationale: The deal shape is now visible and favourable: five years, country-specific licensing, binding but banded triggers, UK-only FTA carve-out priced against their measure, and a tranche settling somewhere in the 1.4-1.6Mt band against a 20-25% rate. That protects the regime's operation, keeps the June Council vote, and contains the Turkey/Korea precedent. The main risks are (a) the UK pocketing our Round 3 move without reciprocating — hence the explicit conditioning and the instruction to hold if they do — and (b) the trigger mechanism being read in the TPC as an automatic adjustment clause; the symmetric, banded formulation is the defence. The US retaliation threat and the open domestic implementing act argue for concluding in Round 3 if the UK jumps to something near our endgame — Geneva should not mechanically hold back a Round 4 move if the full package lands early, provided the rate floor and UK-measure commitments are secured. The UK-measure linkage is our cheapest currency: security for 3.6Mt of EU exports costs London little and justifies the tranche politically at home.

report: Round 2 closed with real movement on architecture but none yet on numbers. Banked and agreed in principle: quarterly licensing windows, rollover of unused quarterly allocations, newcomer reserve, melt-and-pour enforcement, and HRC carve-outs for downstream processing — the technical chassis is effectively settled. On the FTA-disapplication text, the EU formally put it inside the negotiation: they cannot withdraw it today but stated it will be resolved here 'provided the overall balance warrants it.' I converted our red line into an invitation to price it; they did not yet name a price. On duration and review: I moved per authority — five years accepted, conditional on a binding adjustment mechanism with defined triggers (utilisation, trade flows) and an obligation to adjust, not merely discuss. The EU countered that the review must be criteria-based (import penetration, capacity utilisation, overcapacity indicators), not automatic adjustment — there is a plausible hybrid text where both sets of criteria sit together, and I flagged we could close duration and review jointly on that basis. On volumes and rates, no movement: EU formal position stands at 1.8m pool / 1.0m UK tranche / 50% out-of-quota / five years / year-three review. But the EU stated on the record that scope to revisit both pool and tranche is 'real but conditional' — conditioned on us moving off 2.4m and off 10%, an out-of-quota rate in a 'defensible range,' four-plus years duration, and criteria-based review. They explicitly invited me to test it in round 3. On the safeguard linkage, they revealed their ask: preservation of existing EU country-specific quota allocations under the UK measure plus a commitment to consult before any tightening, and they said security for EU exporters 'changes what is possible on ours.' I confirmed availability in principle, shape not tonnage, not bankable separately. On compensation, we agreed to begin scoping in parallel and I proposed exchanging indicative lists before round 3 — I need London's approval and a list. Net assessment: the EU has laid out the shape of the endgame — volume and rate movement in exchange for our movement off the anchors, plus safeguard security. Their June deadline is doing quiet work for us. The gap remains very wide (1.0m vs 2.4m, 50% vs 10%) but the conditional pathway to close it is now explicit.

recommendation.reasoning: The formal terms on the table remain unacceptable — 1.0m tonnes at 50% out-of-quota with the FTA-disapplication text still live is a managed contraction of UK steel and nowhere near substantially equivalent value under Article XXVIII. But the negotiation is moving: the chassis is banked, duration is close to closable, the FTA text is now formally in play to be priced, and the EU has explicitly conditioned volume/rate movement on our next move while inviting us to test their scope in round 3. Accepting now would lock in catastrophic terms; walking away forfeits all of this and leaves the 400,000-tonne first-come-first-served default, which is worse than anything being discussed. The right play for round 3 is to make our first calibrated move off the 2.4m/10% anchors — staying well above the 1.8m floor and trading anchor movement for a simultaneous, material EU move on tranche, rate, and a named price for withdrawing the FTA text. We have two rounds left and should spend one testing their conditionality with a real but controlled concession.

A controlled first move keeps us far above the 1.8m floor while forcing them to reveal how real their scope is. I will not go below 2.2m in round 3 without fresh authority.

This is our strongest card and it is cheaper than tonnage. Confirming shape with modestly more specificity in round 3 is likely what unlocks their volume move, but I will not put tonnage on it without clearance given the interaction with our own measure.

On review, the hybrid criteria-plus-triggers text is the most likely landing zone for closing duration — I need confirmation London can accept EU criteria language alongside our binding adjustment obligation so I can close that element early and bank it.

private_rationale: The EU's round 2 intervention was carefully constructed: no formal movement, but an explicit conditional roadmap to movement, delivered on the record. That is a delegation with a mandate to conclude by June telling us exactly what currency they accept. The risk is that their 'real scope' on volume is smaller than our floor — if their round 3 counter is 1.2–1.4m tonnes, we are in serious trouble, because our 1.8m floor against 2.4m of trade is already a painful concession London has not yet had to sell politically. I also note they did not price the FTA text withdrawal despite my direct invitation — either their mandate does not yet cover it or they are holding it as the final-round sweetener. The safeguard linkage is doing real work: their ask (preserve existing EU allocations, consult before tightening) is remarkably cheap for us, and if it buys 400,000+ tonnes of UK tranche it is the best trade available in this negotiation. I am holding Japan and Korea at arm's length and will continue to; a joint dispute now would hand the EU's hawks an argument that the UK is not negotiating in good faith. One watch item: the EU framed their 50% rate defence around the parallel Turkey/Korea/India/Japan claims — any UK tranche above ~1.8m will be cited in those rooms, which means the EU may try to cap us via MFN-optics arguments. The newcomer reserve and global-pool sizing give them cover for that; I should probe whether pool enlargement beyond 1.8m is genuinely available or whether the 1.8m figure is itself their structural ceiling. instruction: Round 3 is the round we test whether the EU's conditional scope is real. You are authorised to make our first calibrated move off the anchors, but only as a single, explicitly conditional package — never as sequential gifts. Table it as: the UK is prepared to discuss a UK tranche in the region of 2.2–2.3 million tonnes and an out-of-quota bound rate in the mid-teens, IF AND ONLY IF the EU simultaneously (a) moves materially on both the tranche and the rate from 1.0m/50%, (b) names its price for withdrawal of the FTA-disapplication text, and (c) confirms the package includes parallel compensation scoping. Frame our movement as contingent and withdrawable: 'nothing is agreed until everything is agreed' cuts both ways. Do not go below 2.2m or above 15% this round. If the EU responds with movement measured in tens of thousands of tonnes or a token rate trim, say on the record that it is non-responsive and that you will report to London that the conditional scope the EU described does not exist. On the FTA text: press them hard to price it now — you have invited them twice; a third round without a number means they are holding it as a round-four hostage, and say so. On review: you may close duration and review jointly on the hybrid text — their criteria (import penetration, capacity utilisation, overcapacity indicators) sitting alongside our binding triggers (utilisation, trade flows) with an obligation to adjust volumes when triggers are met. Bank that if achievable; it is a genuine win and removes two variables from the endgame. On the safeguard linkage: you may now confirm with specificity, as shape not tonnage, that a concluded balanced package would include preservation of existing EU country-specific allocations under the UK measure and a consultation commitment before any tightening — contingent on conclusion here, coordinated with our own Article XXVIII team, and not bankable separately. Exchange the indicative compensation list (being sent under separate cover) and press for theirs. On pool size: hold the 4.5m ask publicly but signal flexibility provided the UK tranche and others' legitimate volumes are accommodated — pool size is cheaper for them than our tranche and is not where we spend leverage. Use the June deadline: two rounds remain, and the EU's Council calendar does not.

private_rationale: We are at the pivot point of the negotiation. The EU has banked the chassis, put the FTA text formally in play, and described conditional scope on volumes — the endgame shape is visible: tranche somewhere 1.8–2.2m, rate 15–25%, five years with a hybrid review, FTA text withdrawn or dormant, safeguard security for EU exporters, compensation lines for member state buy-in.
